meta.title: Who really said "Computers are like Old Testament gods; lots of rules and no mercy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Joseph Campbell really did call his computer an Old Testament god. But The Power of Myth (1988) prints a longer sentence than the famous one-liner.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Computers are like Old Testament gods; lots of rules and no mercy'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Campbell — from The Power of Myth (1988). The book's actual line is longer than the tidy version everyone quotes.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1904–1987 · American writer & professor of comparative mythology
answer.sourceLine: Campbell said it to Bill Moyers in The Power of Myth, the conversation filmed in 1985 and 1986 and published as a book by Doubleday in 1988. The full text ↗ prints a longer sentence — “it seems to me to be an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy” — and the famous one-liner is that sentence tightened; Wikiquote ↗ files the short form under the 1988 PBS series.

source.excerpt: Yes. But then there comes a time when the machine begins to dictate to you. For example, I have bought this wonderful machine — a computer. Now I am rather an authority on gods, so I identified the machine — it seems to me to be an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy.
trail: The line is filed in the sourced quotes section of Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page ↗, under The Power of Myth (1988) and cited to Episode 2, Chapter 22. It is not under that page’s Disputed heading.

The book carries the same thought in a longer sentence. In the full text at the Internet Archive ↗, Campbell tells Moyers that he has bought a computer and, being “rather an authority on gods,” has identified it as “an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy.”

The first edition is catalogued as Campbell with Moyers, The Power of Myth, New York: Doubleday, 1988 ↗. Editor Betty Sue Flowers records in the same volume that the interviews took place in 1985 and 1986 at Skywalker Ranch and the Museum of Natural History, and that the book weaves in transcript material cut from the six-hour series.

That distinction matters for the shorter wording, because the series aired 21–26 June 1988 ↗ — after Campbell’s death in October 1987 — and the book is a companion to it rather than a transcript of it.
source.cutTag: Chapter I · Myth and the Modern World
source.excerptNote: Campbell is answering Moyers, who has just remarked that machines help us remake the world in our own image. The reply runs straight on into an old joke about President Eisenhower asking a room full of computers whether there is a God — and being told, “Now there is.”

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Who was Joseph Campbell?
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American writer & professor of comparative mythology
author.bio: Joseph Campbell taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College for nearly four decades and spent his career on comparative mythology — the search for the patterns that recur in the sacred stories of unrelated cultures. His best-known book, The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), gave popular culture the “hero’s journey,” and his taped conversations with Bill Moyers became one of the most-watched series in American public television history. He died in Honolulu in October 1987, eight months before that series went to air.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The sentence isn’t quite.
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case for a famous-name quote: nobody else is claiming it. The problem is the wording, not the attribution.

items.who: Joseph Campbell — but not in this sentence
items.why: The book gives Campbell a running answer, not an aphorism: “I have bought this wonderful machine — a computer. Now I am rather an authority on gods, so I identified the machine — it seems to me to be an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy.” You can read it in the full text at the Internet Archive ↗.

Campbell was classifying one machine he had just bought — “an Old Testament god,” “a lot of rules.” The circulating version generalises it to all computers and pluralises the gods. Wikiquote ↗ lists that shorter plural form under the television series.

Aggregators name the title and stop there. A Goodreads search ↗ returns the line credited simply to Joseph Campbell, The Power of Myth — with no chapter, page or episode, and no hint that the book and the broadcast are not the same text.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is genuinely Campbell’s. What the primary text actually records is “it seems to me to be an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy,” in the opening chapter of The Power of Myth (Doubleday, 1988) ↗.

context.heading: An eighty-something mythologist meets his first computer
lead: Campbell was in his early eighties when the interviews were filmed at George Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch in 1985 and 1986, and he had just bought a computer. The gag works because of who is telling it: a man who had spent fifty years cataloguing the gods of the world, looking at a beige box on his desk and placing it, professionally, in the pantheon. The setup is Moyers observing that machines let us remake the world in our own image; Campbell’s reply is that sooner or later the machine starts dictating back.

The passage sits in the book’s opening chapter, “Myth and the Modern World,” inside a run about Star Wars, Faust and the state as a machine. Campbell does not leave the computer as a villain: a beat later he calls what happens on the screen a miracle and describes the inside of the machine as “a whole hierarchy of angels.” The Old Testament line is a joke about rule-following, not a verdict on technology.
context.detailsSummary: Why the book and the broadcast may not match
detailsBody: The book is not a transcript of the series. Editor Betty Sue Flowers explains in her Editor’s Note that roughly twenty-four hours of filming produced far more material than the six-hour broadcast could hold, and that the book weaves in passages cut from the series. That means a line can appear in the book without appearing on screen — and, in principle, the reverse.

Wikiquote assigns the compressed one-liner to Episode 2, Chapter 22 of the series. The Internet Archive copies of the book carry only the longer sentence. Both can be true if Campbell put the thought two ways, which is exactly what a speaker returning to a favourite joke tends to do — but this page does not assert the broadcast wording as confirmed, because the broadcast was not checked.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Computers are like Old Testament gods; lots of rules and no mercy." in its sourced Quotes section, under the heading The Power of Myth (1988), cited to "Episode 2, Chapter 22" — not in the page's Disputed section.

The full text of The Power of Myth prints Campbell's reply to Moyers: "Yes. But then there comes a time when the machine begins to dictate to you. For example; I have bought this wonderful machine -- a computer. Now I am rather an authority on gods, so I identified the machine -- it seems to me to be an Old Testament god with a lot of rules and no mercy." It is followed immediately by the Eisenhower "Now there is" joke, and appears in chapter I, "Myth and the Modern World."

The same volume's Editor's Note by Betty Sue Flowers states the conversation took place in 1985 and 1986 at George Lucas' Skywalker Ranch and later at the Museum of Natural History in New York, that roughly twenty-four hours of filming were reduced for the six-hour PBS series, and that the book weaves in additional transcript material and is a companion to the series rather than a replica of it.
The Power of Myth by Joseph Campbell (interviewee) with Bill Moyers was published New York: Doubleday, 1988, xix + 231 pages, ISBN 0385247745 and others.
The Internet Archive item 'the-power-of-myth' is a copy of The Power of Myth by Joseph Campbell with Bill Moyers, dated 1991, with a full-text djvu.txt available.

The Power of Myth was a six-part PBS documentary series that aired 21–26 June 1988; the companion book was published in 1988 by Doubleday and edited by Betty Sue Flowers; episode 2 is 'The Message of the Myth'; the interviews were recorded at Skywalker Ranch and the American Museum of Natural History; Campbell died in 1987, before the series aired.

Joseph Campbell was born 26 March 1904 in White Plains, New York and died 30 October 1987 in Honolulu; he was an American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College working in comparative mythology and comparative religion.

The compressed wording "Computers are like Old Testament gods; lots of rules and no mercy." circulates on quotation aggregators credited to Joseph Campbell with the source given only as The Power of Myth, without chapter, page or episode.
The Joseph Campbell Foundation presents itself as custodian of Campbell's collected works and collected audio, preserving and sharing his scholarship in comparative mythology.
